title: Decibels, power and RMS
blurb: Use dB ratios, add parallel currents, calculate power, and convert between RMS, peak and peak-to-peak to find PEP.

G5B01.why: Doubling power is **about 3 dB** (halving is −3 dB).
G5B01.trap: 6 dB is two doublings, ×4 in power. 9 dB is ×8.

G5B02.why: Each branch has the same voltage and draws its own current, so total current is the **sum of the branch currents**.
G5B02.trap: Adding branches lowers total resistance, so total current rises.

G5B03.trap: 0.5 is the current in amperes, not watts.

G5B04.trap: 24 W misplaces the decimal. 60 comes from dividing 12 by 0.2.

G5B05.trap: Convert milliamperes to amperes before squaring, or the answer is off by 1,000.

G5B06.trap: Peak-to-peak is not RMS. Halve it to peak, then take 0.707, before squaring.

G5B07.why: The **RMS** value of AC heats a resistor exactly as the same DC voltage would.
G5B07.trap: Peak and peak-to-peak are larger than the heating-equivalent value.

G5B08.trap: 169.7 V is only the peak, not peak-to-peak.

G5B09.trap: 24 V multiplies by 1.414, the wrong direction. 34 V is peak-to-peak.

G5B10.why: 1 dB is a power ratio of 10^(−0.1) = 0.794, so 79.4 % remains and **20.6 %** is lost.
G5B10.trap: Loss is not 10 %. A 3 dB loss would leave 50 %.

G5B11.why: A steady carrier has a constant envelope, so PEP equals average power: ratio **1.00**.
G5B11.trap: 0.707 and 1.414 are voltage factors, not power ratios.

G5B12.trap: 346 V is the peak (245 × 1.414), not RMS.

G5B13.why: An unmodulated carrier has constant amplitude, so PEP = average power = **1,060 W**.
G5B13.trap: PEP only exceeds average power when the amplitude varies.

G5B14.trap: Using 500 V directly gives 5,000 W, eight times too big.
